references.text: The context of the Transfiguration on the mountain, where Jesus took Peter, John, and James up the mountain to pray, and his appearance was transformed.
Peter refers back to the Transfiguration on the mountain as an eyewitness account, where they saw Jesus' glory (δόξα) – the same majesty mentioned in Luke 9:32.
Matthew's parallel account of the Transfiguration on the mountain, where the disciples saw Jesus' glory and the two men (Moses and Elijah) standing with him.
In Gethsemane, Jesus found the disciples asleep, their eyes weighed down by sleep (βεβαρημένοι) – the same word is used in Luke 9:32 to describe Peter's and the others' drowsy state.
A parallel to Matthew's account of the disciples in Gethsemane, where their eyes were heavy with sleep – the same theme as Peter's drowsy condition during the Transfiguration.
John testifies that they saw the glory of the Word (δόξαν), glory as of the only Son from the Father – thematically parallel to the disciples seeing Jesus' divine glory.
Mark's parallel account of the Transfiguration, where Peter, James, and John see Jesus transfigured together with Elijah and Moses.
When Moses came down from Mount Sinai, his face shone after speaking with God – an Old Testament parallel to the divine glory revealed on the mountain of the Transfiguration.
